name: Simon the governor of the temple
charge: Betraying the temple treasury to the king out of a private quarrel; slandering Onias the high priest
summary: Falling out with Onias over the market of the city, Simon of the tribe of Benjamin told the governor of Coelosyria that the treasury at Jerusalem was full of infinite sums and could be brought under the king's power. That report sent Heliodorus. When it failed, Simon slandered Onias as the author of the mischief and had a man of his party commit murders.
offense: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city. When he could not overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius the son of Thraseas and told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. Afterward he slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils, and so proceeded in his malice that murders were committed by one Apollonius, a furious man.
judgment: Onias went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all. Scripture does not record Simon's end; it records that his brother Menelaus bought the priesthood with the same appetite, and how that ended. The law's word on the man who takes a bribe against the innocent, and on the false accuser, stands over him unrecorded.

entries.commentary: Thou shalt not raise a false report, nor put thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness: basically, thou shalt not lie. If you did not see it, do not make up a story like you were there; keep your mouth shut. Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil. Enter not into the path of the wicked; sinners entice, saying come with us, cast in thy lot among us, but walk not thou in the way with them, for their feet run to evil and make haste to shed blood. Many of our young men's lives end short because they follow a multitude to do evil. To be in the midst of the singing, like the whole school hollering fight, fight, fight, is to be in the multitude the Most High warns of; a soul without knowledge of the laws of God hastes with his feet and sins.

Neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause. This deals with judgment: do not be a respecter of persons because a man is poor, as if he is automatically wrong when he brings a matter against a rich man. The judges were charged to hear the small as well as the great. In this corrupt system in Babylon, how innocent or guilty you come out depends on how much lawyer you can afford. Our law was holy and righteous because none of that made a difference: either you were right or you were wrong, whether poor or rich. The Pharisees learned the ways of the heathen and began respecting persons, which the book of James speaks against.

If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again; if thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, thou shalt surely help with him. This enemy that hates you is your brother, your own nation, not the other nations as [Matthew 5:44](/bible/matthew/5#v44) is misconstrued to mean. [Deuteronomy 22:1-4](/bible/deuteronomy/22#v1) proves it, saying the same law with thy brother in the place of thine enemy: thou shalt not see thy brother's ox or sheep go astray; in any case, no matter how you feel, bring them again unto thy brother. And if thou know him not, keep it in thine own house until thy brother seek after it. He is still your brother even if you never grew up with him; that is real love for your own people. Deuteronomy means the second law; it speaks the law plain in case you did not understand it here. Keep [Deuteronomy 22:1-4](/bible/deuteronomy/22#v1) and [Leviticus 19:17-18](/bible/leviticus/19#v17) in your hip pocket with this verse.

Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause: verse six explains verse three again in case you did not catch it, do not be partial in judgment. Keep thee far from a false matter; the innocent and righteous slay thou not, for the Most High will not justify the wicked. Thou shalt take no gift, for the gift blindeth the wise and perverteth the words of the righteous: do not take a bribe when it comes to judgment; be upright and honest.

Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger, for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. This is speaking about us, as [Exodus 22:21](/bible/exodus/22#v21) already laid out with [Leviticus 25:35](/bible/leviticus/25#v35).

Six years thou shalt sow thy land, but the seventh year thou shalt let it rest and lie still, that the poor of thy people may eat, and the beasts of the field after them; likewise the vineyard and the oliveyard. That is mercy from the Lord: in the seventh year the land itself fed the poor. The seventh year ties into the count of the jubilee: seven sabbaths of years to the forty-ninth year, and in the fiftieth year no plowing of the land, which the law takes up later.

Six days do thy work, and on the seventh day rest, that thine ox and thine ass may rest, and the son of thy handmaid and the stranger may be refreshed. The stranger here can be another nation working for you: they too get their due rest on the sabbath. When the Lord sets Israel back up to rule, the nations will kick and scream at first, but once these laws are applied there will be righteousness reigning over the earth like they have never seen, and all will be refreshed on the sabbath, spiritually and physically.

Make no mention of the name of other gods is not saying you cannot pronounce the names Buddha, Allah, Krishna, Ra. Christ himself named Beelzebub, the chief of the devils, a name derived from the Philistine god of Ekron, and Christ did no sin; so the verse cannot mean the bare saying of a name. The Lord says this same thing three ways in this one chapter, and the other two places show the meaning: verse 24, thou shalt not bow down to their gods nor serve them nor do after their works; and verses 32 and 33, thou shalt make no covenant with them nor with their gods, for if thou serve their gods it will surely be a snare unto thee. Make no mention means do not learn how to serve and worship them. Joshua and Deuteronomy double it: neither make mention of the name of their gods, nor cause to swear by them, neither serve them, nor bow yourselves unto them; and if thy brother or son or wife entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, thou shalt not consent. Wherever you are, do not go trying to find out how the nations worship their gods.

Three times thou shalt keep a feast unto me in the year: all the males appeared before the Lord God three times in the year. The feast of unleavened bread is the Passover, kept in the time appointed of the month Abib, the first month of the year, as it is written, the feast of unleavened bread drew nigh, which is called the Passover. None shall appear before me empty: you could not come empty-handed. You brought the tenth of your oil, your wine, whatever was required, for the priests to replenish the storehouses. The feast of harvest, the firstfruits of thy labours, is also known as Pentecost and the feast of weeks; and the feast of ingathering, in the end of the year, is also known as the feast of tabernacles and the feast of booths.

Thou shalt not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread, neither shall the fat of my sacrifice remain until the morning. The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the Lord thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk: the Lord repeats what was read at [Exodus 22:30](/bible/exodus/22#v30), that the young one was not to be taken too young and too soon; it stayed its seven days with his dam before it was given.

Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared. Beware of him, obey his voice, provoke him not, for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him. That Angel is speaking of Christ. If thou indeed obey his voice, I will be an enemy unto thine enemies and an adversary unto thine adversaries. These enemies are not the same enemy of verse four: the enemy of verse four is your brother whom you must help and shew mercy; these enemies in verse 22 the Lord himself deals with and destroys for you.

The Angel goes before Israel unto the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, to cut them off. Thou shalt not bow down to their gods nor serve them nor do after their works, but utterly overthrow them and quite break down their images. Serve the Lord your God, and he shall bless thy bread and thy water, take sickness away from the midst of thee, none casting their young nor barren in the land, and the number of thy days he will fulfil. He drives the nations out by little and little, lest the land become desolate and the beasts multiply, until Israel be increased and inherit the land. The bounds are set from the Red Sea even unto the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert unto the river, the river Euphrates. That little sliver on the map today is not how big Israel is supposed to be: the land was to encompass all the way out to the Euphrates by Babylon, taking in parts of what is Iraq and Iran, and it will be filled one day.

Thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor with their gods. They shall not dwell in thy land, lest they make thee sin against me: for if thou serve their gods, it will surely be a snare unto thee. This is the third way the Lord states the command of verse 13 in this chapter: no learning their worship, no serving, no covenant.

On the day Israel passed over Jordan into the land, they were to set up great stones, plaster them with plaster, and write upon them all the words of this law. Here is the difference between the truth and Islam and every other religion. The stone is not to be worshipped or thought to be a god; you set it up and put the laws on it so you can remember the laws.

The stones were to be set up in mount Ebal, and an altar of whole stones built there unto the Most High; no iron tool was to be lifted upon them. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were offered there, and the people were to eat and rejoice before the Most High. Thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly. That is what the Most High wants remembered most: not the stone itself, but the law written on it.

Moses and the priests the Levites told all Israel: this day thou art become the people of the Lord thy God; therefore obey his voice and do his commandments and statutes. Even the other nations' own books witness to it. The Martyrdom of Man says that "God made all men equal" is a fine sounding phrase but not a scientific fact, and that those who outlive hardships and sufferings which fall on all alike owe their existence to some superiority not only of body but of mind. There is no way we could have lasted this long through what we have been through if we were not the people of the Most High: thousands of years run out of the homeland, living among our enemies, put on ships and transported all over the world, and still surviving from 1492 on up here in Babylon the great.

Moses charged the people that day: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph (which is Ephraim and Manasseh), and Benjamin were to stand upon mount Gerizim to bless the people. Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali were to stand upon mount Ebal to curse. Half the tribes stood on one side and half on the other, one saying one thing and the other answering.

The Levites were to speak with a loud voice unto all the men of Israel: cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the Most High, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place. And all the people shall answer and say, Amen. Every curse that follows carried that same answer from the whole congregation.
Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother. Setting light by them means disrespecting your parents and not obeying them.

Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark. Every man in Israel was allotted a certain plot of land for his inheritance individually. If you moved that landmark trying to make your own land bigger, the Most High says cursed be upon you. The allotments are recorded in Joshua and in [Numbers 27](/bible/numbers/27), where the inheritance laws are given.
Cursed be he that maketh the blind to wander out of the way. Do not mistreat those we call the disabled.

Cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow. This goes back to Deuteronomy chapter 1, where the judges were charged to judge righteously between every man and his brother and the stranger with him, and to respect no persons in judgment.
Cursed be he that lieth with his father's wife, because he uncovereth his father's skirt. That is nasty stuff, and the curse of the whole congregation stood against it.
Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast. Bestiality is the practice of Esau, and Israel was cursed for touching it.
Cursed be he that lieth with his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother. This goes back to Leviticus chapter 18, where the nakedness laws were first given.
Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law, and all the people shall say, Amen. Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, and all the people shall say, Amen.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. That is your hitman right there in verse 25: taking payment to kill the innocent puts you under the curse.

Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. At that time this encompassed everything, including the law of sacrifice. It also applies to us today, because sacrifice is alive and well; it just transformed. We still sacrifice, only it is no longer animals but our bodies. Our bodies must be holy and without blemish before the Most High, because the law says you cannot bring anything with blemishes into the house of the Lord. If your sacrifice is not holy and acceptable, the Son is not taking you to present you before the Father. Christ magnified the law, as Isaiah says.

verses.text: But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city.
And when he could not overcome Onias, he gat him to Apollonius the son of Thraseas, who then was governor of Celosyria and Phenice,

And told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not pertain to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the king’s hand.

Now when Apollonius came to the king, and had shewed him of the money whereof he was told, the king chose out Heliodorus his treasurer, and sent him with a commandment to bring him the foresaid money.
So forthwith Heliodorus took his journey; under a colour of visiting the cities of Celosyria and Phenice, but indeed to fulfil the king’s purpose.
This Simon now, of whom we spake afore, having been a betrayer of the money, and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and been the worker of these evils.
Thus was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws.
But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed,
Onias seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius, as being the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, did rage, and increase Simon’s malice,
He went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private:
For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.
Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon’s brother, to bear the money unto the king, and to put him in mind of certain necessary matters.
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. And all the people shall say, Amen.
